rounds.t: Heart tube, outflow tract, valves, and septation

q.s: In vertebrate embryos, the heart is the first functional organ. By approximately which week of development does it begin to beat spontaneously?
e: At 2 weeks the embryo is still bilaminar; there is no heart tube yet.
Correct. The heart beats spontaneously by about 4–5 weeks of development.
By week 8 the heart has been beating for several weeks.
Week 12 is well into the fetal period.
Fetal heart activity is detectable months before this.

q.s: Cardiac looping of the primary heart tube establishes which property of the heart, and when does it begin?
e: Valves arise from endocardial cushions later.
Outflow tract septation depends on neural crest cells, not looping.
Correct. Looping establishes left–right polarity and begins in week 4 of development.
Septation follows looping and is not what looping establishes.
Coronary vessels are not established by looping.

q.s: A 9-year-old boy has chronic sinusitis, recurrent bronchiectasis, and heart sounds loudest on the right side of the chest. A defect in which protein explains his cardiac position?
e: Elastin defects cause supravalvular aortic stenosis (Williams syndrome).
Type III collagen defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Correct. Defective left–right dynein (Kartagener syndrome) disrupts cardiac looping asymmetry and can cause dextrocardia.
Fibrillin defects cause Marfan syndrome, with aortic root dilation, not dextrocardia.
Dystrophin defects cause muscular dystrophy and cardiomyopathy, not dextrocardia.

q.s: The truncal and bulbar ridges spiral and fuse to form the aorticopulmonary septum. Which cell population must migrate for this to occur?
e: Foregut endoderm forms GI and respiratory epithelium.
Surface ectoderm forms epidermis and lens, not cardiac septa.
Intermediate mesoderm forms the kidneys and gonads.
Correct. Neural crest cell migration forms the truncal and bulbar ridges that build the aorticopulmonary septum.
Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, not the outflow septum.

q.s: The aorticopulmonary septum divides the truncus arteriosus into which two structures?
e: Correct. The aorticopulmonary septum separates the ascending aorta from the pulmonary trunk.
Ventricles are separated by the interventricular septum.
These derive from pharyngeal arch arteries.
These are venous structures not derived from the truncus.
Coronary arteries are not formed by septation of the truncus.

q.s: Which group of congenital heart defects is associated with failure of neural crest cell migration?
o: Coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve
Hypoplastic left heart and mitral atresia
Transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, and persistent truncus arteriosus
e: These are valvular anomalies.
These are not the conotruncal group listed.
These are not attributed to neural crest migration failure.
These are not classified as conotruncal neural crest defects.
Correct. These conotruncal abnormalities result from failure of neural crest migration.

q.s: A newborn is cyanotic and echocardiography shows a single great vessel arising from both ventricles. The defect most directly reflects failure of which embryologic process?
o: Formation of the aorticopulmonary septum by migrating neural crest cells
e: This produces a PFO, not a single outflow vessel.
Correct. Persistent truncus arteriosus results when the aorticopulmonary septum fails to form, a neural crest migration defect.
Looping defects cause dextrocardia.
Cushion failure causes AV septal defects.
Muscular VSDs do not create a single great vessel.

q.s: The aortic and pulmonary valves are derived from which embryologic structure?
o: Endocardial cushions of the outflow tract
Fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal
e: The sinus venosus forms the smooth RA and coronary sinus.
Correct. Semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves derive from endocardial cushions of the outflow tract.
These give rise to the mitral and tricuspid valves.
The bulbus cordis forms smooth outflow portions of the ventricles, not valves.
Septum primum contributes to the atrial septum and foramen ovale flap.

q.s: The mitral and tricuspid valves develop from which structure?
o: Fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal
Endocardial cushions of the outflow tract
e: Correct. The AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves derive from fused endocardial cushions of the AV canal.
Truncal ridges form the aorticopulmonary septum.
This forms the smooth part of the LA.
These form the semilunar valves.
Septum secundum is part of atrial septation.

q.s: An infant has a downward-displaced tricuspid valve with atrialization of part of the right ventricle. This valvular anomaly is best classified as:
e: Atresia is absence of the valve opening, eg, tricuspid atresia.
Regurgitation may occur, but the defining feature is displacement.
Bicuspid refers to an abnormal number of cusps, typically of the aortic valve.
Stenosis is a narrowed valve orifice.
Correct. Ebstein anomaly is a displaced valve anomaly.

q.s: During atrial septation, how does the ostium secundum form?
o: Cell death creates an opening in the septum primum as the ostium primum regresses
Septum primum fuses with the muscular ventricular septum
Septum secundum grows over the ostium primum
The sinus venosus is absorbed into the RA
e: Correct. Ostium secundum forms within septum primum by cell death.
Cushion fusion failure causes AV septal defects.
Septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions, not the ventricular septum.
Septum secundum later covers most of the ostium secundum.
That forms the smooth part of the RA, not the ostium secundum.

q.s: Septum secundum develops on which side of septum primum, and what residual opening does it leave?
e: The side is wrong; septum secundum lies to the right.
The interventricular foramen lies between the ventricles.
Correct. Septum secundum grows on the right side of septum primum and covers most of the ostium secundum, leaving the foramen ovale.
Septum secundum develops on the right, and the residual opening is the foramen ovale.
Ostium primum regresses before septum secundum covers the ostium secundum.

q.s: After birth, what forms the one-way flap valve of the foramen ovale?
o: The remaining portion of septum primum
e: Septum secundum forms the rigid upper rim.
This marks the boundary of the smooth and trabeculated RA.
This directs IVC blood toward the foramen ovale but is not its flap.
Correct. The remnant of septum primum forms the one-way valve of the foramen ovale.
The cushions contribute to the lower atrial septum and AV valves.

q.s: Soon after birth, septum primum closes against septum secundum, sealing the foramen ovale. Which pressure change causes this closure?
e: Pulmonary pressure falls after the first breath.
Placental separation actually ↑ systemic resistance.
IVC return falls when umbilical flow stops.
This would push the flap open, maintaining a right-to-left shunt.
Correct. ↑ LA pressure and ↓ RA pressure push septum primum against septum secundum.

q.s: A 38-year-old woman has a stroke after a long flight. Bubble study shows right-to-left flow across the atrial septum with Valsalva. Failure of which embryologic event explains this finding?
o: Spiral fusion of the truncal ridges
Growth of the muscular interventricular septum
Fusion of septum primum and septum secundum after birth
e: This creates the aorticopulmonary septum.
Ostium secundum formation is normal; its absence would not cause this.
A VSD is between the ventricles.
Correct. Patent foramen ovale results from failure of the two septa to fuse and can allow paradoxical emboli.
Cushion failure causes AV septal defects.

q.s: Patent foramen ovale is present in roughly what proportion of the population?
e: PFO is far more common than this.
PFO is more common than 5%.
Correct. About 25% of the population has a PFO; most are asymptomatic and undetected.
This overestimates the prevalence.
This greatly overestimates the prevalence.

q.s: Which is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly, and where does it usually occur?
e: TOF is the most common cyanotic lesion, not the most common anomaly overall.
Correct. VSD is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly and usually occurs in the membranous septum.
VSDs usually occur in the membranous, not muscular, septum.
PDA is common but not the most common.
ASDs are common but less so than VSDs.

q.s: The membranous interventricular septum closes the interventricular foramen. It forms from fusion of the aorticopulmonary septum with the muscular septum, plus contributions from which structure?
e: Correct. Endocardial cushions contribute to the membranous ventricular septum and separate the atria from the ventricles.
The bulbus forms smooth outflow tracts.
Septum secundum is atrial.
The sinus venosus contributes to the RA and coronary sinus.
This forms the smooth LA.

q.s: A 3-month-old with Down syndrome has a common AV valve with both an ASD and a VSD. This complete atrioventricular septal defect results from:
o: Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions
Failure of septum primum and secundum to fuse
e: This causes a secundum ASD.
Correct. AV septal (endocardial cushion) defects result from incomplete cushion fusion; they are associated with Down syndrome.
This causes conotruncal defects.
Looping defects cause dextrocardia.
This causes a PFO.

q.s: A partial atrioventricular septal defect characteristically includes which combination?
o: Primum ASD with cleft mitral valve and no VSD
Common AV valve, ASD, and VSD
e: This is not an AVSD.
These are unrelated defects.
Correct. Partial AVSD: primum ASD with a cleft mitral valve (causing mitral regurgitation) and no VSD.
This describes a complete AV septal defect.
Secundum defects are not endocardial cushion defects.

q.s: The superior vena cava develops from which embryonic veins?
o: Left horn of the sinus venosus
Right common and anterior cardinal veins
e: This forms the coronary sinus.
Correct. The SVC derives from the right common/anterior cardinal veins.
This forms the smooth part of the LA.
These form the IVC.
Vitelline veins contribute to hepatic portal structures, not the SVC.

q.s: The inferior vena cava is formed from which embryonic venous system?
o: Right horn of the sinus venosus
Posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins
e: This forms the smooth part of the RA.
The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
This is arterial and forms the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
Correct. These veins together give rise to the IVC.
This contributes to the SVC.

q.s: The coronary sinus is derived from which embryonic structure?
o: Left horn of the sinus venosus
Right horn of the sinus venosus
e: This is not the listed source of the coronary sinus.
This forms ventricular outflow tracts.
Correct. The left horn of the sinus venosus becomes the coronary sinus.
The right horn forms the smooth part of the RA (sinus venarum).
This forms the trabeculated parts of both atria.

q.s: The smooth-walled portion of the right atrium (sinus venarum) comes from:
o: Left horn of the sinus venosus
Right horn of the sinus venosus
e: This forms the coronary sinus.
This forms the smooth part of the LA.
Cushions form septa and valves.
Correct. The right horn of the sinus venosus forms the smooth part of the RA.
The primitive atrium forms the trabeculated parts of the atria.

q.s: The smooth part of the left atrium is derived from which structure?
o: Left horn of the sinus venosus
e: Correct. The primitive pulmonary vein is incorporated into the LA to form its smooth part.
This forms the great arteries.
This becomes the coronary sinus.
The primitive atrium forms the trabeculated LA (auricle).
Septum primum forms part of the atrial septum.

q.s: The trabeculated parts of the left and right ventricles derive from the primitive ventricle. What gives rise to the smooth outflow portions of both ventricles?
e: This forms venous inflow structures.
Cushions form valves and membranous septa.
The truncus forms the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
This forms trabeculated atrial tissue.
Correct. The bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow tracts of the LV and RV.

q.s: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the atrial septum, membranous interventricular septum, and the AV and semilunar valves?
e: This forms the smooth RA and coronary sinus.
This forms the great arteries.
This forms the trabeculated ventricles.
The bulbus forms the outflow tracts.
Correct. Endocardial cushions contribute to the atrial septum, membranous IV septum, and AV and semilunar valves.

q.s: The trabeculated portions of both atria derive from:
e: This forms the smooth LA.
This forms outflow tracts.
This forms trabeculated ventricles.
Correct. The primitive atrium forms the trabeculated parts of the LA and RA.
The sinus venosus forms the smooth RA.

q.s: During thyroidectomy, a surgeon notes a fibrous band connecting the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch, lying close to a nerve that loops beneath it. Which nerve is at risk near this ligament?
e: The vagus passes nearby, but the classic relationship is with its left recurrent laryngeal branch.
Correct. The ligamentum arteriosum (from the ductus arteriosus) lies near the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The thoracic duct is not the nerve associated with this ligament.
This nerve loops under the right subclavian artery.
The phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root.

q.s: The ductus venosus becomes which postnatal structure?
e: This is the remnant of the foramen ovale.
This is the remnant of the umbilical arteries.
This is the remnant of the umbilical vein.
This is the remnant of the urachus.
Correct. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.

q.s: A 6-week-old has urine leaking from the umbilicus. Failure of obliteration of which structure explains this, and what is its normal adult remnant?
e: A patent vitelline duct drains meconium, not urine.
Correct. The urachus, part of the allantois between bladder and umbilicus, normally becomes the median umbilical ligament.
These carry blood, not urine.
This is a hepatic vascular shunt.
A patent umbilical vein does not leak urine.

q.s: The ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament) is the remnant of which fetal vessel, and where does it run?
o: Umbilical vein; within the falciform ligament
Umbilical artery; within the medial umbilical fold
Ductus arteriosus; near the aortic arch
Allantois; within the median umbilical fold
Ductus venosus; within the lesser omentum
e: Correct. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, contained in the falciform ligament.
Umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.
This becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
The allantois/urachus becomes the median umbilical ligament.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.

q.s: The medial umbilical ligaments are remnants of the:
e: This becomes the median umbilical ligament.
This becomes the ligamentum teres.
These are not the source of the medial umbilical ligaments.
This becomes the ligamentum venosum.
Correct. The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.

q.s: In fetal circulation, oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein bypasses the hepatic circulation by passing through which shunt into the IVC?
e: This shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta.
Correct. Umbilical vein → ductus venosus → IVC bypasses the liver.
Blood through the portal vein enters the liver rather than bypassing it.
The foramen ovale shunts blood from RA to LA.
These carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

q.s: In the fetus, most of the highly oxygenated blood arriving in the IVC is directed to the left atrium through which route?
e: Fetal lungs receive little flow and add no oxygen.
The coronary sinus drains myocardial venous blood into the RA.
Correct. Most highly oxygenated IVC blood passes through the foramen ovale into the LA.
This carries mainly SVC-derived deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta.
This directs umbilical vein blood into the IVC, upstream of the heart.

q.s: Deoxygenated blood from the fetal SVC enters the RV and is shunted from the pulmonary artery through the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta. Why does this shunt occur?
o: ↑ LA pressure relative to RA pressure
e: High prostaglandin levels keep the ductus open.
In the fetus RA pressure exceeds LA pressure.
Correct. High fetal pulmonary vascular resistance diverts RV output through the ductus arteriosus.
Pulmonary resistance is high, not low, in the fetus.
The placenta keeps fetal systemic resistance low.

q.s: Which pair of changes at birth leads to closure of the ductus arteriosus?
o: ↑ O2 from respiration and ↓ prostaglandins from placental separation
e: Correct. Rising O2 and falling prostaglandins close the ductus arteriosus.
These close the foramen ovale, not the ductus.
Pulmonary resistance falls with the first breath.
These would keep the ductus open.
Umbilical flow stops at birth.

q.s: A premature infant has a continuous machine-like murmur and bounding pulses. Echocardiography confirms a patent ductus arteriosus. Which drug would help close it?
e: Correct. NSAIDs such as indomethacin or ibuprofen, or acetaminophen, help close a PDA ("endomethacin ends the PDA").
Digoxin does not close the ductus.
Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog and would keep the ductus open.
PGE1 keeps the ductus open.
Inhaled nitric oxide lowers pulmonary resistance; it is not used to close a PDA.

q.s: A newborn with transposition of the great arteries depends on the ductus arteriosus for mixing. Which agent keeps the ductus patent until surgery?
e: Acetaminophen can help close a PDA.
Ibuprofen closes the ductus.
↑ O2 promotes ductal closure.
Correct. PGE1 and PGE2 keep the PDA open.
Indomethacin closes the ductus.

q.s: During a cardiac surgery, an oval depression is seen on the interatrial septum of the right atrium. This structure is the postnatal remnant of which fetal structure?
e: The ostium primum regresses during septation and leaves no named depression.
The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
Correct. The foramen ovale closes after birth to become the fossa ovalis.
The sinus venosus contributes to the smooth RA wall and coronary sinus.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum in the liver.
